wb-beamish-acorn-6393.analysis.WHODAS_SC.title: BHS Analysis — WHODAS 2.0 Scores
wb-beamish-acorn-6393.analysis.WHODAS_SC.description: Calculated summary scores from the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0) 12-item short form — one row per participant per visit. Contains the simple sum score (whodas_s_sum) derived from items Q1-Q12, plus three self-reported overall health-impact items: number of days difficulties were present (whodas_h1), number of days totally unable to function (whodas_h2), and number of days with reduced activity due to health conditions (whodas_h3). The summary score ranges from 0 (no disability) to 48 (maximum disability). This table aggregates data from both CRF and App survey administrations (indicated by survey_format). For item-level raw responses, see bhs.crf.WHODAS or bhs.appsurveys.WHODASA. Cross-study note: WHODAS is a WHO-standardized instrument — scores are directly comparable across studies using the same short form. BHS uses USUBJID while PRESCO uses participant_id.

wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.EQ5D.title: BHS CRF — EQ-5D-5L (Quality of Life)
wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.EQ5D.description: EuroQol 5-Dimension 5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) — a standardized measure of health-related quality of life. Captures five dimensions: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression, each scored on a 1–5 severity scale (1 = no problems, 5 = extreme problems/unable). Includes a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for overall health today rated 0–100. The anxiety/depression dimension is critical for cross-study analysis with PHQ-9 and GAD-7 for comprehensive mental health profiling. The EQ-5D can also be used alongside WHODAS to provide complementary functional status and quality-of-life assessments. Cross-study note: EQ-5D functional dimensions can be compared conceptually with PRESCO participant functional outcomes for evaluating post-COVID quality of life.

wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.GAD7.title: BHS CRF — GAD-7 (Anxiety Screening)
wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.GAD7.description: Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7) — a validated, 7-item self-report anxiety screener administered at BHS clinical visits. Each item assesses the frequency of a specific anxiety symptom over the past 2 weeks on a 0–3 Likert scale (0 = Not at all, 1 = Several days, 2 = More than half the days, 3 = Nearly every day). Total score ranges from 0 to 21 with clinical severity cutoffs: 5 = mild, 10 = moderate, 15 = severe anxiety. The GAD-7 is a primary mental health outcome measure in BHS and is typically analyzed alongside PHQ-9 (depression) for comprehensive behavioral health profiling. The EQ-5D anxiety/depression dimension provides complementary quality-of-life context. Cross-study note: while PRESCO does not include GAD-7 directly, anxiety phenotyping from BHS can inform post-COVID outcome analyses.

columns.name: gad7_2
columns.description: Not being able to stop worrying

wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PFT.title: BHS CRF — PFT (Pulmonary Function Tests / Spirometry)
wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PFT.description: Pulmonary Function Tests (PFT / Spirometry) — device-measured lung function assessments performed at BHS clinical visits per ATS/ERS standards. Key measures include FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second), FVC (forced vital capacity), FEV1/FVC ratio, DLCO (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide), and flow rates at various lung volumes (FEF25, FEF50, FEF75, FEF25-75). An FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70 suggests obstructive lung disease (e.g., COPD, asthma). Percent-predicted values (fvcpre, pefpre, dlcopre) normalize for age, sex, height, and ethnicity. PFT data are critical for respiratory phenotyping in BHS and relate to PRESCO post-COVID respiratory outcomes analyses. Cross-study note: BHS PFT provides objective lung function baselines that can be compared to post-COVID respiratory sequelae characterized in PRESCO.

wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PHQ9.title: BHS CRF — PHQ-9 (Depression Screening)
wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PHQ9.description: Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) — a validated, 9-item self-report depression screener administered at BHS clinical visits. Each of the 9 items assesses the frequency of a specific depressive symptom over the past 2 weeks on a 0–3 Likert scale (0 = Not at all, 1 = Several days, 2 = More than half the days, 3 = Nearly every day). Total score ranges from 0 to 27 with clinical severity cutoffs: 5 = mild, 10 = moderate, 15 = moderately severe, 20 = severe depression. Item 10 captures functional impairment caused by endorsed symptoms. The PHQ-9 is one of the primary mental health outcome measures in BHS and can be analyzed alongside GAD-7 (anxiety) and EQ-5D (quality of life) for comprehensive behavioral health profiling. Cross-study note: while PRESCO does not include PHQ-9 directly, depression/anxiety phenotyping from BHS can inform post-COVID outcome analyses when cohort criteria are applied consistently.

wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.WHODAS.title: BHS CRF — WHODAS 2.0 (WHO Disability Assessment Schedule)
wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.WHODAS.description: WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0, 12-item short form (WHODAS 2.0) — a self-report measure of functional disability across six domains: cognition (S3, S6), mobility (S1, S7), self-care (S8, S9), getting along (S10, S11), life activities (S2, S12), and participation (S4, S5). Each of the 12 items (S1–S12) is scored on a 5-point scale: 1 = None, 2 = Mild, 3 = Moderate, 4 = Severe, 5 = Extreme/Cannot do (codes 0–4). Items H1–H3 capture total days with difficulties, days unable to function, and days with reduced activity in the past 30 days. The WHODAS raw item responses are used to compute the summary score in bhs.analysis.WHODAS_SCORES. Longitudinal changes in WHODAS indicate functional recovery or decline. Cross-study note: BHS WHODAS functional disability maps conceptually to PRESCO progressor status for evaluating post-COVID functional outcomes.

columns.name: whodas_s12
columns.description: Day to day work (S12 — Life Activities)

wb-beamish-acorn-6393.screener.DM.title: BHS Screener — Demographics (DM)
wb-beamish-acorn-6393.screener.DM.description: Participant demographics collected during BHS screening — one row per participant. Contains age at enrollment, sex at birth, current gender identity alignment, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, self-identified race, study recruitment source, and participation motivations. This table is essential for cohort characterization, stratification, and subgroup analyses across all BHS tables. Demographics are needed to normalize clinical measurements (e.g., PFT percent-predicted values depend on age, sex, and ethnicity). Cross-study note: BHS uses USUBJID while PRESCO uses participant_id — no direct patient overlap between studies, but demographic criteria can be applied consistently for comparable cohort definitions.

wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.cell_subs.title: PRESCO — Cell Subset Frequencies
wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.cell_subs.description: Calculated immune cell subset frequencies for PRESCO participants — derived from flow/mass cytometry gating strategies. Each row represents the calculated frequency of a specific immune cell subset (e.g., Naive CD4+ T cells, Classical monocytes) for one participant at one visit. The subset_code links to subset_code_name_mapping for full names and marker definitions.

wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.participa.title: PRESCO — Participant Info
wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.participa.description: Participant demographics and clinical status for the PRESCO (Post-COVID Recovery) immune profiling study. Includes PASC (Long COVID) classification and Progressor status from the CPR publication. This table is the identity anchor for all PRESCO omic data — participant_id links to subset_id (prefix) in ATACseq, RNAseq, TaPEseq and to sample_id (prefix) in cell_subset_frequencies.

wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.rnaseq.title: PRESCO — RNAseq Gene Expression
wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.rnaseq.description: RNA-seq gene expression values for PRESCO immune cell subsets — measures transcript abundance per gene per cell subset. Each row contains read counts (for association analysis) and TPM (Transcripts Per Million, for cross-sample comparison) for one gene in one immune cell subset sample. Gene IDs follow Gencode Release 24, with additional ERCC spike-in RNA controls.

results.question: How many people screened positive for depression?
results.sql:
WITH
  phq9_scores AS (
    SELECT
      USUBJID,
      (
        IFNULL(phq9_1_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_2_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_3_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_4_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_5_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_6_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_7_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_8_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_9_CODE, 0)
      ) AS phq9_total_score
    FROM
      `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PHQ9`
  )
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT t.USUBJID) AS total_participants_with_phq9,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN t.phq9_total_score >= 10 THEN t.USUBJID END) AS participants_screened_positive
FROM
  phq9_scores AS t;
results.response_text:
The query has finished. Here are the results:

Out of **1,449** total participants who completed a PHQ-9 depression questionnaire, **132** participants screened positive for at least moderate depression (a score of 10 or greater) on at least one occasion.

**A few important notes on this result:**

*   This number represents anyone who screened positive at *any* point during the study, not necessarily that they have a formal diagnosis of depression.
*   The PHQ-9 is a screening tool, not a diagnostic tool.
*   The participant identifier (`USUBJID`) used in this query is a sensitive, unique ID.

Would you like to explore the depression scores further? For example, we could look at the distribution of scores, or see how many participants screened positive at their first visit versus later visits.

results.question: Show the distribution of disability severity
results.sql:
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN whodas_s_sum = 0 THEN 'No disability'
    WHEN whodas_s_sum BETWEEN 1 AND 12 THEN 'Mild disability'
    WHEN whodas_s_sum BETWEEN 13 AND 24 THEN 'Moderate disability'
    WHEN whodas_s_sum >= 25 THEN 'Severe/Extreme disability'
    ELSE 'Unknown'
  END AS disability_severity,
  COUNT(DISTINCT USUBJID) AS number_of_participants
FROM
  `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.analysis.WHODAS_SCORES`
WHERE
  whodas_s_sum IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY
  1
ORDER BY
  CASE
    WHEN disability_severity = 'No disability' THEN 1
    WHEN disability_severity = 'Mild disability' THEN 2
    WHEN disability_severity = 'Moderate disability' THEN 3
    WHEN disability_severity = 'Severe/Extreme disability' THEN 4
    ELSE 5
  END;
results.response_text:
The query has successfully executed and here is the distribution of disability severity among the participants in the Baseline Health Study (BHS):

| Disability Severity       | Number of Participants |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| No disability             | 1545                   |
| Mild disability           | 2004                   |
| Moderate disability       | 397                    |
| Severe/Extreme disability | 72                     |

As you can see, the majority of participants report no or mild disability, with a smaller number reporting moderate to severe disability.

**A note on the data:** This analysis is based on the `whodas_s_sum` score, which is a self-reported measure of functional disability. The `USUBJID` column used to count participants is a unique identifier and is considered sensitive data ([UID]).

You could explore this further by looking at how disability severity correlates with other factors like age, specific medical conditions, or quality of life scores. For example, we could investigate the distribution of diagnoses within each disability category.

Let me know if you would like to explore any of these follow-up questions

results.question: Do we have lung function measurements? What's the average?
results.sql:
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT USUBJID) AS number_of_participants,
  AVG(fev1) AS average_fev1,
  AVG(fvc) AS average_fvc,
  AVG(ratio) AS average_fev1_fvc_ratio,
  AVG(dlco) AS average_dlco
FROM
  `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PFT`
WHERE
  pft_perf = 'Y' AND pft_qual = 'Satisfactory'
results.response_text:
### **Results**

The query returned the following average lung function values based on data from **2,316** participants in the BHS study:

*   **Average FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1s):** 3.08 L
*   **Average FVC (Forced Vital Capacity):** 4.05 L
*   **Average FEV1/FVC Ratio:** 75.86%
*   **Average DLCO (Diffusing Capacity of the Lungs for Carbon Monoxide):** 22.55 mL/min/mmHg

### **Limitations**

*   These averages are calculated across all participants and do not account for individual factors like age, sex, and height, which significantly influence lung function.
*   This data is from the Baseline Health Study (BHS) only. The PRESCO study does not contain these direct PFT measurements.

### **Next Steps**

We could refine this analysis. For example, we could investigate if these lung function metrics differ between smokers and non-smokers. Would you be interested in exploring that?

results.question: How does self-reported quality of life vary by visit?
results.sql:
SELECT
    t.VISIT,
    t.VISITNUM,
    COUNT(t.USUBJID) AS participant_count,
    AVG(SAFE_CAST(t.eq5d_health AS FLOAT64)) AS avg_health_vas,
    AVG(t.eq5d_mobi_CODE) AS avg_mobility,
    AVG(t.eq5d_selfcare_CODE) AS avg_selfcare,
    AVG(t.eq5d_usual_CODE) AS avg_usual_activities,
    AVG(t.eq5d_paindis_CODE) AS avg_pain_discomfort,
    AVG(t.eq5d_anxiety_CODE) AS avg_anxiety_depression
FROM
    `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.EQ5D` AS t
WHERE
    t.VISIT IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY
    t.VISIT,
    t.VISITNUM
ORDER BY
    t.VISITNUM
LIMIT 100
results.response_text:
### Summary of Results

The results show the average self-reported quality of life scores across five annual study visits for participants in the BHS study.

*   **Overall Health (avg_health_vas)**: The average self-rated health score on the 0-100 VAS scale is quite stable, remaining high around **81-83** across all visits. There is a slight decrease in the year four visit.
*   **Health Dimensions**: The average scores for the five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) are all low (typically between 1.0 and 1.7). Since a score of 1 indicates "no problems" and 2 indicates "slight problems," this suggests that the participant population, on average, reports having only slight issues across these domains. The scores remain fairly consistent over the first four years of the study.

### Limitations

*   This analysis only includes data from the Baseline Health Study (BHS), as the PRESCO study does not contain this specific quality of life instrument.
*   The number of participants decreases at later visits, which could influence the averages.

### Follow-up Suggestions

Would you like to:
1.  Investigate if these quality of life scores differ for participants with specific health conditions, such as a history of cardiovascular disease (`der_hx_cvd` in the `DIAGNOSES` table)?
2.  Explore the distribution of scores for a specific dimension, like anxiety/depression, to see how many participants report moderate to severe problems?

results.question: Show me alcohol screening results
results.sql:
SELECT
    t1.USUBJID,
    t1.VISIT,
    t1.study_day,
    t1.AUDITC_SUM_SCORE
  FROM
    `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.analysis.AUDITC_SCORES` AS t1
  WHERE
    t1.AUDITC_SUM_SCORE IS NOT NULL
  ORDER BY
    t1.USUBJID,
    t1.VISITNUM
  LIMIT 100
results.response_text:
This table shows the AUDIT-C scores for each participant (`USUBJID`) at different study visits (e.g., `STUDY_START`, `YEAR_ONE_ANNUAL_VISIT`). As you can see, the scores are captured longitudinally throughout the study.

**Interpreting the Scores:**
*   **Score Range:** 0 to 12.
*   **Hazardous Drinking:** Scores ≥ 3 for women or ≥ 4 for men are generally considered to indicate hazardous drinking or active alcohol use disorders.

results.question: Are people with depression also more likely to have anxiety?
results.sql:
WITH DepressionAndAnxietyScores AS (
    SELECT
        phq9.USUBJID,
        (phq9.phq9_1_CODE + phq9.phq9_2_CODE + phq9.phq9_3_CODE + phq9.phq9_4_CODE + phq9.phq9_5_CODE + phq9.phq9_6_CODE + phq9.phq9_7_CODE + phq9.phq9_8_CODE + phq9.phq9_9_CODE) AS phq9_score,
        (gad7.gad7_1_CODE + gad7.gad7_2_CODE + gad7.gad7_3_CODE + gad7.gad7_4_CODE + gad7.gad7_5_CODE + gad7.gad7_6_CODE + gad7.gad7_7_CODE) AS gad7_score
    FROM
        `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PHQ9` AS phq9
    INNER JOIN
        `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.GAD7` AS gad7
    ON
        phq9.USUBJID = gad7.USUBJID AND phq9.VISIT = gad7.VISIT
)
SELECT
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN phq9_score >= 10 THEN USUBJID END) AS num_with_depression,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN gad7_score >= 10 THEN USUBJID END) AS num_with_anxiety,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN phq9_score >= 10 AND gad7_score >= 10 THEN USUBJID END) AS num_with_both
FROM
    DepressionAndAnxietyScores
LIMIT 1000
results.response_text:
The results are in. Based on the screening questionnaires:

*   **132** participants met the criteria for moderate to severe depression.
*   **120** participants met the criteria for moderate to severe anxiety.
*   **76** participants met the criteria for *both* conditions.

This indicates a significant overlap. Specifically, **approximately 58% of participants with depression (76 out of 132) also show signs of moderate to severe anxiety.**

This suggests a strong correlation between depressive and anxious symptoms in this cohort.

**Limitations**:

*   This analysis is based on self-reported screening questionnaires (PHQ-9 and GAD-7), not clinical diagnoses.
*   This is a cross-sectional look at the data and doesn't imply causation.

**Next Steps**:

We could further investigate this relationship by:

*   Examining the severity of symptoms in the co-morbid group.
*   Analyzing the demographic characteristics of this group.
*   Exploring how these scores change over time for individuals.

results.question: Is there a relationship between lung function and disability?

results.question: Do participants with more diagnoses have worse quality of life?
results.sql:
SELECT

        IFNULL(t1.der_hx_arrythmia, 0) +

        IFNULL(t1.der_hx_pad, 0) +
        IFNULL(t1.der_hx_vhd, 0) +
        IFNULL(t1.der_hx_htn, 0) +
        IFNULL(t1.der_hx_diab, 0) +
        IFNULL(t1.der_hx_dyslipidemia, 0) +
        IFNULL(t1.der_hx_ckd, 0)
    ) AS diagnosis_count,

    ON t1.USUBJID = t2.USUBJID AND t1.VISIT = t2.VISIT
WHERE
    t1.VISIT = 'STUDY_START'
    AND t2.eq5d_health IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY
    diagnosis_count DESC
LIMIT 100
results.response_text:
### Results:

The query successfully returned 100 participants, ordered by the number of diagnosed conditions.

*   Another participant with 8 diagnoses (`BL001-001-7626127183`) has a score of 60.
*   As the `diagnosis_count` decreases, the `quality_of_life_score` tends to vary widely, but we see many scores in the 80s, 90s, and even 100. For example, a participant with 6 diagnoses (`BL001-001-3165540670`) reported a perfect quality of life score of 100.

This initial exploration suggests a potential trend that a higher number of diagnoses may be associated with a lower quality of life score, but the relationship is not perfectly linear.

### Limitations:

*   This analysis is a simple correlation and does not imply causation.
*   The `diagnosis_count` is based on a specific set of 13 derived diagnosis flags and is not an exhaustive count of all possible medical conditions.
*   The quality of life score is a subjective, self-reported measure.
*   The `USUBJID` is a sensitive column containing a unique identifier for each participant.

### Follow-up Suggestions:

2.  We could investigate the impact of specific diagnoses (e.g., `der_hx_chf` - congestive heart failure) on quality of life, rather than just the total count.

results.question: Show immune cell subset frequencies for PASC versus non-PASC participants

**Limitations:**

results.question: Build me a combined mental health cohort across both studies
results.sql:
-- Define a cohort of BHS participants with mental health conditions
-- This includes moderate/severe depression or anxiety, or a history of major depression/bipolar disorder.
SELECT
    DISTINCT USUBJID,
    'BHS' AS study
FROM (
    -- Participants with moderate to severe depression (PHQ-9 score >= 10)
    SELECT USUBJID FROM `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.PHQ9`
    WHERE (
        IFNULL(phq9_1_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_2_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_3_CODE, 0) +
        IFNULL(phq9_4_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_5_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_6_CODE, 0) +
        IFNULL(phq9_7_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_8_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(phq9_9_CODE, 0)
    ) >= 10

    UNION DISTINCT

    -- Participants with moderate to severe anxiety (GAD-7 score >= 10)
    SELECT USUBJID FROM `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.crf.GAD7`
    WHERE (
        IFNULL(gad7_1_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(gad7_2_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(gad7_3_CODE, 0) +
        IFNULL(gad7_4_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(gad7_5_CODE, 0) + IFNULL(gad7_6_CODE, 0) +
        IFNULL(gad7_7_CODE, 0)
    ) >= 10

    UNION DISTINCT

    -- Participants with a medical history of major depression or bipolar disorder
    SELECT USUBJID FROM `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.analysis.DIAGNOSES`
    WHERE mh_major_depression = 1 OR mh_bipolar = 1
)
LIMIT 100

    WHERE
      (
        t2.gad7_1_CODE + t2.gad7_2_CODE + t2.gad7_3_CODE + t2.gad7_4_CODE + t2.gad7_5_CODE + t2.gad7_6_CODE + t2.gad7_7_CODE
      ) >= 10
  ),
  physical_impairment AS (
    SELECT
      t3.USUBJID
    FROM
      `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.analysis.WHODAS_SCORES` AS t3
    WHERE
      t3.whodas_s_sum > 10
  )
SELECT
  t4.USUBJID
FROM
  mental_impairment AS t4
  INNER JOIN physical_impairment AS t5 ON t4.USUBJID = t5.USUBJID
LIMIT 100
results.response_text:
The query successfully returned a list of 100 participant IDs (`USUBJID`) who show evidence of both physical and mental health impairment.

**Limitations & Caveats:**

*   The definitions of "impairment" are based on commonly used, but not universally applicable, clinical cutoffs.
*   This analysis only includes data from the BHS study.
*   The participant IDs are sensitive information and should be handled accordingly.

**Next Steps:**

You could now:

*   Investigate the specific diagnoses or demographic characteristics of this cohort.
*   Explore the severity of their physical and mental health impairments.
*   Analyze how these impairments change over time.

results.question: Compare disability scores between the two study populations
results.sql:
SELECT
    'PRESCO' AS study,
    COUNTIF(pasc = 1) AS pasc_participant_count,
    COUNT(participant_id) AS total_participants,
    SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(pasc = 1), COUNT(participant_id)) * 100 AS pasc_percentage
  FROM
    `wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.participant_info`
results.response_text:
### Summary of Results

*   **BHS Study**: Among 2,484 participants, the average WHODAS 2.0 disability score is **3.65** (on a scale of 0 to 48). This suggests a relatively low level of functional disability in the general population cohort.
*   **PRESCO Study**: In the post-COVID recovery cohort of 232 participants, **36.6%** (85 individuals) are classified as having PASC (Long COVID), indicating a significant portion of this study group is experiencing lasting effects from the infection.

### Limitations

It is important to reiterate that these two metrics are not directly comparable. The BHS study measures general functional disability in a broad population, while the PRESCO study identifies a specific post-infectious condition (Long COVID) as a binary outcome.

### Follow-up Suggestions

1.  We could investigate the distribution of WHODAS scores within the BHS cohort to see how many participants fall into different severity levels.
2.  We could explore the demographic or clinical characteristics of the participants with PASC in the PRESCO study to better understand this subgroup.

results.question: What biological and clinical data exists across studies for COVID recovery research?

What data do we have on respiratory outcomes?
results.sql:
SELECT
    pft.USUBJID,
    pft.VISIT,
    dm.age_at_enrollment,
    dm.SEX,
    pft.fev1,
    pft.fvc,

LIMIT 10;
results.response_text:
### **Results**

The query returned key pulmonary function measurements for 10 participants from the BHS study. For each participant (`USUBJID`), we can see their age and sex, along with their FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC ratio at a specific `VISIT`.

For example, participant `BL001-001-2798623060` (a 56-year-old male) has an FEV1/FVC ratio of 53%, which is below the typical threshold of 70% and may suggest an obstructive respiratory pattern. In contrast, participant `BL001-001-7101580213` (a 22-year-old male) has a ratio of 95%, which is well within the normal range.

### **Limitations**

*   This data is from the BHS study only. The PRESCO study does not contain direct PFT measurements, though it does characterize participants based on post-COVID outcomes, which can have respiratory components.
*   The interpretation of PFT values is highly dependent on population-specific reference equations (percent-predicted values), which account for age, sex, height, and ethnicity. The query above shows the raw values; a more in-depth analysis would involve using columns like `fvcpre` (FVC percent predicted) and `dlcopre` (DLCO percent predicted) from the `PFT` table.

### **Follow-up Suggestions**

1.  We could investigate the distribution of the FEV1/FVC `ratio` across the entire cohort to identify the prevalence of potential obstructive lung disease.
2.  We could correlate these PFT results with smoking history (`smoking_status`, `pack_years_smoked`) from the `wb-beamish-acorn-6393.analysis.DIAGNOSES` table to explore risk factors.

results.question: Can we link participants across the two studies?
results.response_text:
No, it is not possible to directly link individual participants across the BHS and PRESCO studies.

Here’s why:

*   **Different Participant IDs**: The two studies use completely different, non-overlapping identification systems.
    *   The **BHS** study (from the `wb-beamish-acorn-6393` project) uses the `USUBJID` column to identify participants.
    *   The **PRESCO** study (from the `wb-glittery-carrot-8816` project) uses the `participant_id` column.

There is no mapping table or shared identifier that connects a `USUBJID` from BHS to a `participant_id` in PRESCO.

### What this means for analysis:

You cannot track a single individual's journey from the BHS study to the PRESCO study. Instead, you can compare **groups of similar people** (cohorts) from each study.

For example, you could define a cohort of "females aged 50-60 with a history of hypertension" in both the BHS and PRESCO datasets, and then analyze and compare their outcomes independently within each study. This allows you to look for similar patterns and trends across the two different populations.

results.question: I want to study recovery trajectories — what's available?
results.sql:
SELECT
    t1.sample_id,
    SPLIT(t1.sample_id, '_')[OFFSET(1)] AS visit_number,
    t2.pasc AS long_covid_status,
    t1.subset_code,
    t1.freq
FROM
    `wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.cell_subset_frequencies` AS t1
INNER JOIN
    `wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.participant_info` AS t2 ON SPLIT(t1.sample_id, '_')[OFFSET(0)] = t2.participant_id
WHERE
    t1.subset_code = 'T4nv' -- Naive CD4+ T cells
    AND t2.participant_id IN (SELECT participant_id FROM `wb-glittery-carrot-8816.presco.participant_info` LIMIT 10)
ORDER BY
    t1.sample_id
LIMIT 100
results.response_text:
*   **Results**: This query shows the frequency (`freq`) of a specific T cell subset for participants at different visits. You can see each participant's `long_covid_status` (1 = yes, 0 = no). By comparing these frequencies across visits for participants with and without Long COVID, you can investigate the immunological basis of recovery.
*   **Next Steps**: You could expand this query to include multiple time points for the same individuals to visualize the trajectory, or you could look at different immune cell subsets.

In summary, you have rich data in both studies to explore recovery. I recommend starting with these examples and then we can refine the queries to focus on specific conditions, timeframes, or populations.

results.question: Which tables should I use if I'm writing a grant about post-COVID disability?
results.sql:
SELECT
